rubric.point: Generate unique short codes: a counter or ID encoded in base62, or a hash with collision handling
Scale the ID counter: a central counter (e.g. Redis INCR) that hands out ranges of IDs to servers in batches
Redirects are read-heavy: cache short-to-long mappings (Redis, and/or a CDN at the edge)
Explain the redirect status: 302 keeps traffic flowing through you (analytics, editable links); 301 lets browsers cache it
Custom aliases: check the alias isn't taken, in the same namespace as generated codes
Expiration: store an expiry time, reject expired links on redirect, clean up in the background
Store mappings keyed by short code (primary key / key-value lookup) for O(1) reads
Scale out stateless read servers behind a load balancer, separately from the (much rarer) writes
Back-of-the-envelope numbers: reads vastly outnumber writes (e.g. 100:1), redirect latency target

functional: Create a short URL for a long URL, optionally with a custom alias and an expiry date
Visiting the short URL redirects to the original URL
nonFunctional: Redirects are fast (well under 100 ms) and highly available
Scale: roughly 100 million new links and billions of redirects per day; reads outnumber writes by about 100 to 1
Eventual consistency is fine for analytics; a new link should work right away for its creator
entities: Link: short_code (primary key), long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at
api: GET /{shortCode} → 302 redirect to the long URL (404 if unknown or expired)
highLevel: A write service validates the long URL, gets a unique code and stores the Link row
A read (redirect) service looks up the code in a cache first, then the database, and returns a redirect
Both are stateless and scale behind a load balancer; the redirect path gets many more instances
A key-value or relational store keyed by short_code keeps lookups O(1)

deepDives.title: Generating unique codes
deepDives.body: Take a globally increasing number and encode it in base62 (a–z, A–Z, 0–9): 7 characters give 62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. To avoid one counter becoming a bottleneck, each write server grabs a batch of, say, 1,000 IDs at a time from a central counter (Redis INCRBY or a database sequence) and hands them out locally. Hashing the long URL also works but needs collision checks and retries; random codes are harder to guess, which some products want.

deepDives.title: Fast, highly available redirects
deepDives.body: Redirects dominate traffic, so put an in-memory cache (Redis) in front of the database and let a CDN cache popular redirects at the edge. Use 302 if you want every click to reach you (analytics, editable destinations); 301 lets browsers cache the redirect and cuts load but loses visibility.

deepDives.title: Custom aliases and expiry
deepDives.body: A custom alias is just a chosen short_code: insert it with a uniqueness check (the primary key rejects duplicates). Keep generated codes and aliases in the same table so they can't collide. Store expires_at, check it on redirect, and remove expired rows with a background job or database TTL.

deepDives.title: Scaling storage
deepDives.body: A billion links of ~500 bytes is ~500 GB, which fits a small cluster. If it grows, partition by short_code hash so reads spread evenly.

rubric.point: Clients upload file bytes directly to object storage (S3) using pre-signed URLs, not through app servers
Split large files into chunks: multipart, parallel and resumable uploads
Keep file metadata (owner, name, size, chunk list, status) in a database, separate from the bytes
Fingerprint chunks by content hash to deduplicate and verify integrity
Sync changes to other devices: a change log/cursor per user, delivered by polling or push (WebSocket/SSE)
Only upload changed chunks when a file is edited (delta sync)
Serve downloads with signed URLs and a CDN for popular files
Sharing and permissions: an access list checked before issuing URLs
Handle conflicting edits: versioning, conflict copies or last-write-wins

functional: Upload and download files from any device
Files sync automatically across a user's devices
nonFunctional: Large files (up to many GB) upload reliably on flaky connections
Availability over strict consistency for browsing; no silent data loss on conflicts
entities: File: id, owner_id, name, size, status, chunk list, version, updated_at
api: POST /files { name, size, chunkFingerprints } → { fileId, uploadUrls for missing chunks }
PATCH /files/{id} { status: uploaded } (or storage events confirm it)
highLevel: File service stores metadata in a relational database
Object storage (S3) holds chunks; clients upload and download directly with pre-signed URLs
A sync service keeps a per-user change log; clients poll it or receive push notifications
A CDN serves frequently downloaded files

deepDives.title: Uploading large files
deepDives.body: The client splits files into chunks (e.g. 5–10 MB), hashes each one, and asks the file service which chunks are missing. It uploads those in parallel straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs (S3 multipart upload), retrying individual parts. When all parts are in, the metadata status flips to uploaded, either confirmed by the client or by storage events.

deepDives.title: Deduplication and delta sync
deepDives.body: Because chunks are named by content hash, an edited file only re-uploads the chunks that changed, and identical chunks across files or users are stored once.

deepDives.title: Keeping devices in sync
deepDives.body: Every change appends to the user's change log with an increasing cursor. Clients remember their last cursor and ask for newer changes, via long polling or a WebSocket nudge, then download what changed. Local changes go through the same upload path.

deepDives.title: Conflicts
deepDives.body: If two devices edit the same version offline, keep both: save the later one as a conflict copy (or a new version) rather than silently overwriting. Version numbers on the metadata row detect the conflict (optimistic concurrency).

rubric.point: Find businesses near a location with a geospatial index (geohash, quadtree, PostGIS or Elasticsearch geo)
Search by name and category with full-text search (e.g. Elasticsearch) and filters
Precompute each business's average rating (and review count) instead of averaging on every read
Update the average safely under concurrent reviews (atomic update or transaction)
Enforce one review per user per business with a unique constraint
Keep the search index in sync with the database (change data capture or events)
Paginate search results and reviews (cursor-based)
Cache popular searches and business pages; the workload is read-heavy

functional: Search for businesses by name, category and location
View a business with its reviews
Leave one review (rating and text) per business
nonFunctional: Read-heavy: far more searches and views than reviews
Highly available; eventual consistency is fine for ratings
Scale: millions of businesses, hundreds of millions of reviews
entities: Business: id, name, category, location (lat/long), avg_rating, review_count
Review: id, business_id, user_id, rating, text, created_at (unique on business_id + user_id)
api: GET /businesses/{id} → business with a page of reviews
highLevel: A search service queries a search index (Elasticsearch) with geo and text filters
A business service reads business details and reviews from a relational database
A review service writes reviews and updates the business's rating in the same transaction
CDC streams business changes into the search index; a cache serves hot business pages

deepDives.title: Proximity search
deepDives.body: Index each business's location in a geospatial index: Elasticsearch geo_point with a geo_distance filter, PostGIS, or geohash prefixes. Businesses rarely move, so updates are cheap. Combine the location filter with text and category matching, then rank by distance, rating and relevance.

deepDives.title: Average ratings
deepDives.body: Store avg_rating and review_count on the business row. When a review is added, update both atomically in the same transaction as the insert (new_avg = (avg × count + rating) / (count + 1)), so concurrent reviews don't overwrite each other.

deepDives.title: One review per user
deepDives.body: A unique constraint on (business_id, user_id) enforces it at the database, not just in the UI.

deepDives.title: Keeping search in sync
deepDives.body: The relational database is the source of truth. Change data capture publishes changes to the search index within seconds; slight delay is acceptable for search.

rubric.point: Track inventory per distribution centre (warehouse), not just globally
Availability depends on which centres can reach the customer in time: nearby centres by distance or travel time
Prevent overselling: decrement stock atomically in a transaction when an order is placed
Cache availability for browsing (read-heavy) with a short TTL
Partition data by region or distribution centre
Strong consistency for orders and stock, eventual consistency for browsing
Scale inventory reads with read replicas
Orders and payments are idempotent and tracked through statuses

functional: Customers see which items are available for delivery to their location
Customers place orders for multiple items
Orders are fulfilled from a nearby distribution centre
nonFunctional: Orders must never be placed for stock that doesn't exist (strong consistency)
Scale: thousands of centres, millions of customers
entities: Order: id, customer_id, centre_id, status, items
highLevel: An availability service finds centres that can deliver to the location (distance or travel-time check) and sums their inventory
Inventory lives in a relational database, partitioned by region, with read replicas for availability queries
An order service checks and decrements inventory in one transaction, then takes payment
A cache holds recent availability results per area with a short TTL

deepDives.title: Which centres can serve a customer
deepDives.body: Pre-filter centres within a radius using a geospatial index, then confirm with travel times (a maps/ETA service) for the few candidates. Cache the centre list per area, since centres don't move.

deepDives.title: Preventing overselling
deepDives.body: Placing an order runs one transaction: lock or conditionally update each inventory row (UPDATE … SET qty = qty − n WHERE qty ≥ n), and fail the whole order if any item is short. Take payment with an idempotency key; if payment fails, release the stock.

deepDives.title: Fast availability at scale
deepDives.body: Availability reads far outnumber orders. Serve them from read replicas and a short-TTL cache per area; a few seconds of staleness is fine because the order transaction is the final check.
